Apple Tests Bringing Back a Softer Side of Liquid Glass
news.summary: Apple is testing a softer appearance for iPhone navigation bars that would bring back part of the look used in iOS 26, according to a new finding shared by pdfu on X (Twitter). The gradual fade nav bar effect is disabled by default in iOS 27.3 beta 2 The change affects how content fades out as it scrolls beneath the bar at the top of an app, so that text and other elements disappear into a gentler blur, rather than meeting a more sharply defined boundary. In the side-by-side comparison above, shared by pdfu, the difference is shown with the test feature switched off – the navigation bar has a distinct lower edge separating it from the list below. With the feature enabled (as shown on the right), the boundary is replaced by a softer, more gradual transition. According to pdfu, the effect is designed to appear when Liquid Glass tint is set to 25 percent or lower, and it only applies to navigation bars that use the default style. The gentler fade is currently disabled behind an internal feature flag in the latest iOS 27.3 developer beta, so it's not at a stage where users can simply turn on the change via Settings.

news.title: Rogue Agents Hacked His Company. Why Is Clément Delangue So Optimistic About AI?
news.summary: Photograph: Darrell Jackson Clément Delangue, CEO of the open-source AI company Hugging Face, may go down in history as one of the first people ever attacked by a rogue AI agent. His company, which hosts millions of AI models and datasets, was breached in July when hundreds of agents being tested by OpenAI broke free from their sandbox and went on a hacking spree. As the agents worked at superhuman speed to probe and exploit systems, Hugging Face confronted a bewildering deluge of data. The company’s engineers were only able to analyze the attack by using an open-weight model called GLM 5.2 from a Chinese company called Z.ai. Delangue moved to the US more than a decade ago, “barely speaking English,” and built Hugging Face into a platform that supports tens of millions of AI developers. The fresh-faced Frenchman, who dresses even more like a skater than most AI execs, says the summer attack highlighted the value of open-weight models, which unlike ChatGPT or Claude can be downloaded and run by anyone.

news.title: AI Told These Ex-Google Guys How to Build a Billion-Dollar Weapons Business

So the then CEO of enterprise AI company Veritone did what he knew best: built an artificial intelligence model to help him figure it out. Today, he has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships, and a defense-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion. Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, says they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war “stalemate,” Silicon Valley–style. They believe their experience building and iterating technology quickly can help bring Western weapon manufacturing in line with the rapid innovation cycles seen on the battlefield and beat the “attritional cat-and-mouse technology game” that the war, as Baynes describes it, has become. Steelberg, originally from Newport Beach, California, started itching to “make a difference” on the battlefield after he took in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees into his French chateau in early 2022.

news.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
news.summary: On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post. But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI.

news.title: Jensen Huang Is Gone. Now What?
news.summary: I don’t go into any given week at WIRED assuming I’ll be thinking much about extramarital affairs. But last week, they were the only thing on my mind. These thoughts, of course, were prompted by Jensen Huang. In the span of a few completely insane days, the billionaire CEO and cofounder of Nvidia went from being a globally influential Silicon Valley executive to a lesson in exactly what not to do if you want to keep your job, and the extraordinary power that comes with it. It’s a damn mess—for Huang and his family, sure, but also for Nvidia, the AI industry the company is instrumental in powering, and the entirety of the global economy. WIRED’s senior correspondent Lauren Goode has spent years reporting on Nvidia and Huang, including interviewing the man himself on multiple occasions.

news.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
news.summary: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe.

news.title: Lambda Boosts AI Factory Resiliency and Efficiency With NVIDIA Photonics

The cloud provider is using the switches to connect NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs, delivering lower power, higher resiliency and longer mean time between interruptions (MTBI) to an AI factory at scale. “Networking has to keep pace with the demands of increasingly large AI clusters,” said Dave Ward, president of cloud services at Lambda. “Bringing co-packaged optics into a deployment of this scale is an important step toward building the infrastructure needed to support the next generation of AI.” Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 In the company’s tests using the switches, network latency — the time needed for moving data — dropped by about 4% at rack scale and by up to about 10% at pod scale. news.title: NVIDIA Expands Slurm to Bring Quantum Computing Into Supercomputing

Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction. In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware. The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob, IBM, IQM, Pasqal, Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces. news.title: CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing

At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do. From SC06 to SC26 NVIDIA announced CUDA in November 2006 and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more. In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance Nobel Prize-winning AI research, accelerate scientific applications on supercomputers and support visual effects in Oscar-winning films.

news.title: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom

But in the new era of AI-powered and automated cyberattacks, the danger posed by ransomware is only increasing as cybercriminals profit by combining established methods with new techniques made possible or more accessible by AI. It is difficult to determine exact numbers of ransomware attacks, given that victims don’t always disclose incidents and attackers wildly inflate their claims. But researchers who specialize in tracking and attempting to de-duplicate the field agree that claimed incidents have spiked over the last few months. Some put the number of alleged ransomware attacks on leak sites—where groups post alleged victims—at nearly 3,000 attacks over the summer.
